claims.text: Chemical short-range order governs phase stability in near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Chemical short-range order governs the combined high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Nanoscale SRO stabilizes a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a predominantly disordered ductile matrix and finely distributed ordered clusters.
A cast near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy can have a nearly random solid solution with minimal preexisting SRO.
Annealing Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni at 600–800 °C will produce moderate nanoscale SRO relative to rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching will retain a random Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni solid solution with minimal SRO.
SRO formation reduces lattice distortion and locally lowers free energy.
The local reduction in lattice distortion and free energy stabilizes the proposed dual-phase microstructure.
Ordered SRO clusters impede dislocation motion and thereby strengthen the alloy.
Ordered clusters promote preferential segregation of oxide-forming elements and protective oxide formation.
SRO clusters act as effective sinks for radiation-induced defects.
Moderate SRO prevents large brittle ordered regions from forming at cryogenic temperatures while preserving a ductile matrix.
The annealed SRO-rich samples will have approximately 10–20% greater high-temperature yield strength than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The annealed SRO-rich samples will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics and more protective oxide formation than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The annealed SRO-rich samples will accumulate fewer irradiation-induced voids or dislocation loops than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The annealed SRO-rich samples will have improved cryogenic toughness because moderate SRO avoids embrittling overordering.
The hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni between room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
The proposed benefits may fail when SRO becomes excessively extensive or composition departs significantly from the near-equiatomic state.
Prior evidence from another high-entropy alloy qualitatively supports SRO-mediated dislocation strengthening.
